name: Glycolic acid

lead: Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid and one of the most widely used chemical exfoliants. Lower-strength products are used at home for dullness and rough texture, and higher concentrations are applied in professional peels.
Studies show improvements in photoaged skin texture and fine lines with regular use, although stronger peels carry greater risk.

paras: By weakening the bonds between surface skin cells, glycolic acid promotes exfoliation, and with repeated use it stimulates epidermal renewal and has been reported to increase dermal collagen and glycosaminoglycans.

Stinging, redness and peeling are frequent, and the skin becomes more sensitive to ultraviolet light, so sunscreen use is advised. Excess strength or poor technique can cause burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin tones.

lead: Glycolic acid (hydroxyacetic acid, HOCH2COOH) is the smallest alpha hydroxy acid (AHA). It is a colorless, odorless, water-soluble crystalline solid that occurs in sugarcane, sugar beets, pineapple, unripe grapes and other plants, and is also made industrially [1][1]. In skin care and dermatology it is used as a chemical exfoliant, both in home products at low concentrations and in higher-strength professional peels [2][3].

Its main cosmetic uses are for dull or rough skin, photoaging, uneven pigmentation such as melasma, and as an adjunct for acne marks and stretch marks. A 2024 systematic review of chemical peels for melasma, covering 24 studies with 1,075 participants, concluded that glycolic acid was the most safe and effective peeling agent among those studied, although the studies were too heterogeneous to pool [4].

Glycolic acid is an irritant. Product labels and reviews describe stinging, redness and peeling as common effects, and label warnings advise sun protection because AHAs can increase sun sensitivity [5]. The peel literature links peel depth to both results and complications [6].
infobox: Sugarcane, sugar beet, pineapple, unripe grapes
Cosmetic and OTC products; stronger peels used by clinicians

paras: Glycolic acid is sold in cleansers, toners, pads, serums and leave-on treatments aimed at dullness, rough texture, clogged pores and signs of photoaging. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes concentrations of 5 to 10 percent in cosmetics as promoting epidermal renewal and improving texture and tone [7]. Professional peels use higher concentrations and are applied by clinicians; reviews describe them as a superficial resurfacing procedure [6][2].

In pigmentation, a 2024 review describes glycolic acid among peeling agents used as additional or maintenance therapy for melasma [8]. A review of striae distensae (stretch marks) lists glycolic acid among commonly cited topical treatments, alongside tretinoin and ascorbic acid, while noting the lack of strong evidence for any treatment [9].

On T Nation, a poster in a thread of life tips says that skin products containing AHAs such as lactic, malic and glycolic acid make skin look noticeably better and that science backs this, particularly for glycolic acid [10]. Another poster comments that creams containing cheap ingredients such as retinoids or glycolic acid are heavily marked up [11].

The strongest summarized evidence concerns melasma. In a 2024 systematic review, prospective case series and randomized trials of chemical peels were assessed with self-ratings, physician global assessment and the Melasma Area and Severity Index; the authors reported glycolic acid as the safest and most effective peel in that setting [4]. A separate 2024 narrative review says peels are an adjunct or maintenance option rather than a primary therapy [8].

A 2013 review of glycolic acid peel therapy is available in the open literature, and a 1996 editorial in Dermatologic Surgery discussed glycolic acid peels [2][12]. Laboratory work on human skin explants has examined pH-adjusted glycolic acid and collagen production and epidermal renewal [13]. A 2018 review addresses the dual effects of alpha hydroxy acids on skin [3].

Wikipedia characterizes glycolic acid as a skin irritant [1]. A retail glycolic acid exfoliating pad listed in the US DailyMed database carries external-use-only warnings, advises stopping if redness, itching or irritation develop, advises against use on broken skin, suggests starting with use once or twice a week, and carries a sunburn alert recommending SPF 30 or higher [5]. Grokipedia likewise says AHAs increase photosensitivity [7].

A 2009 study examined the effects of topical glycolic acid and salicylic acid on ultraviolet radiation-induced erythema, DNA damage and sunburn cell formation in human skin [14]. The Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology review of superficial and medium-depth peels states that peel depth is directly related to both results and complications [6].

Burns and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are recognized complications of peeling, and the peel literature links peel depth to complication risk [6][8]. Grokipedia also notes that ingesting ethylene glycol leads to glycolic acid and oxalate, with kidney risk, which concerns systemic exposure rather than cosmetic use [7].

As a keratolytic, glycolic acid weakens attachments between surface skin cells to promote exfoliation. Grokipedia attributes its depth of penetration to its small molecular size and describes stimulation of collagen production [7]. A laboratory study titled for glycolic acid adjusted to pH 4 reported collagen and epidermal renewal effects in skin explants without raising TNF-alpha, as its title indicates [13]. Peel strength depends on concentration, formulation pH and contact time, according to the peeling literature [6][2].

Glycolic acid is slightly stronger than acetic acid because of the electron-withdrawing hydroxyl group, with a pKa near 3.8 [1][7]. It is produced industrially mainly by carbonylation of formaldehyde, and also from chloroacetic acid and sodium hydroxide [1]. It is a monomer for polyglycolic acid and poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) (PLGA), biodegradable polymers that are the subject of a large separate literature on drug delivery and implants, which is distinct from topical glycolic acid [1][15].

Auguste Laurent coined the name in 1848, proposing it as the hypothetical acid related to glycine. Adolph Strecker and Nikolai Sokolov first prepared it in 1851 [1]. Its adoption in dermatology came much later; a 1996 editorial in Dermatologic Surgery already discussed glycolic acid peels as an established procedure [12].

Glycolic acid features in the community material reviewed mostly in passing, within general fitness forums, as one of the cheap, widely sold exfoliating actives. Posters compare it with retinoids as inexpensive ingredients backed by data and note the price premium on branded creams [10][11].

Human research includes a 2024 systematic review of 24 melasma peel studies (9 clinical or comparative trials and 15 randomized controlled trials, 1,075 participants in total, 8 to 36 weeks), which named glycolic acid the safest and most effective peeling agent [4]. A 2000 randomized trial tested hydroquinone cream with or without salicylic acid peels for photodamage of the neck and chest, rather than glycolic acid itself [16]. A 2025 randomized trial examined an AGE-inhibiting moisturizer's effect on procedure effectiveness [17].

Registered trials include a single 70 percent glycolic acid peel with vitamin C for photoaging and for acne scars (small studies of 10 participants each), a withdrawn trial of glycolic-salicylic versus glycolic peel for melasma, a pilot comparison of salicylic and glycolic peels in melasma, a trial of modified Jessner's solution or glycolic acid combined with trichloroacetic acid in melasma, and a study in acquired epidermodysplasia verruciformis in HIV-infected children [18][19][20][21][22][23].
